subject: science
title: Reading Weather Patterns
objective: Use weather data to describe patterns and predict short-term changes.

visual.title: Weather systems image
visual.caption: A map-style weather visual with pressure zones, wind arrows, clouds, and temperature bands.

teachingSupport.summary: Weather predictions are evidence claims built from patterns in pressure, temperature, wind, and clouds.
teachingSupport.description: Learners read a map like a forecast team: gather data, make a claim, test confidence, and revise after actual weather arrives.

diagramCallouts.title: Pressure zone
diagramCallouts.body: High and low pressure help explain likely air movement and changing conditions.

diagramCallouts.title: Wind arrow
diagramCallouts.body: Wind direction helps predict what kind of air may arrive next.

diagramCallouts.title: Evidence claim
diagramCallouts.body: A forecast should cite at least two pieces of current map or table evidence.

helperNotes: Ask students to separate observation, pattern, and prediction.
Require a confidence rating so teams notice missing or weak evidence.
After real weather happens, revise the rule instead of only marking right or wrong.

commonMisunderstandings.mistake: Using one symbol as a complete forecast.
commonMisunderstandings.fix: Ask for two data points before accepting the claim.

commonMisunderstandings.mistake: Thinking a wrong forecast means the method failed.
commonMisunderstandings.fix: Compare prediction to actuals and improve the rule using new evidence.

teachingSupport.confusionPrompt: Write whether you are stuck on pressure, wind arrows, data tables, or turning evidence into a forecast.

funTasks: Run a forecast studio: one student reads the map, one checks evidence, one records the prediction.
Create a 30-second weather briefing with one claim and two evidence points.
Compare two forecasts and decide which one deserves the team confidence badge.

groupHomework.title: Family weather crew
groupHomework.sharedOutcome: Submit a one-week weather board with predictions, actuals, and one improved forecast rule.
groupHomework.parentRole: Help gather daily observations, but let students defend the forecast.

reward: Earn the Forecast Crew badge when the team improves its rule after real data.

sections.warmup: Look at a three-day temperature and cloud-cover chart.
sections.teach: Weather patterns form when air pressure, temperature, humidity, and wind interact.
sections.guidedPractice: Match symbols on a weather map to observations.
sections.independentPractice: Use a data table to write a two-sentence forecast.
sections.activity: Build a weather station log for one week.
sections.reteach: Review one variable at a time before combining the full forecast.
sections.challenge: Compare forecast confidence when one data point is missing.

quiz.prompt: Which evidence best supports a short-term weather forecast?
choices: A drawing of clouds from last year
quiz.explanation: Current pressure patterns are evidence scientists use to forecast weather.

quiz.prompt: A falling air pressure reading often suggests what kind of change?
quiz.explanation: Falling pressure can indicate approaching unsettled or stormy weather.

studentFacing.mission: Run a forecast studio: make a claim, cite the map, then revise with real data.
studentFacing.whyItMatters: Forecasting teaches evidence reasoning: your claim is only as strong as the data you use.
studentFacing.bigIdea: Weather predictions are claims built from patterns in pressure, wind, temperature, and clouds.
modelSteps: Use at least two data points before making a claim.
Give a confidence rating and name what data is missing.
studentFacing.example: Falling pressure plus changing wind direction can support a claim that unsettled weather may arrive.
studentFacing.nonExample: One cloud icon by itself is not enough evidence for a complete forecast.
studentFacing.quickCheck: Can your forecast sentence include 'because' followed by two pieces of evidence?
studentFacing.studentSummary: A forecast is an evidence claim, not a guess.
studentFacing.tutorHandoff: Tell the tutor if pressure, wind arrows, data tables, or evidence sentences are confusing.

learningObjective: Use weather data to describe patterns and predict short-term changes.
successCriteria: I can separate weather observations from forecast predictions.
I can use at least two pieces of weather evidence before making a claim.
I can explain how pressure, wind, temperature, or clouds support a short-term forecast.
I can revise a forecast rule after comparing it with real weather data.
essentialQuestion: How can weather data support a forecast without turning the forecast into a guess?

knowledge: Weather data includes pressure, temperature, humidity, wind, clouds, and recent change over time.
Forecasts are evidence claims with uncertainty, not guaranteed answers.
capability: Read a weather map or table and identify at least two useful data points.
Write a short forecast claim with evidence and confidence.
reasoning: Compare strong and weak forecast evidence.
Revise a rule when actual weather does not match the forecast.
retention: Recall what high/low pressure and wind arrows can indicate after a delay.
transfer: Use the same evidence logic on a new city, map, or weather table.

phaseModules.title: Join the forecast studio
phaseModules.studentAction: Study the mission and write one thing a forecast must prove with evidence.
phaseModules.successCheck: The learner can say the lesson is about evidence-based prediction, not guessing.

phaseModules.title: Read the weather map like data
phaseModules.studentAction: Inspect the pressure zones, wind arrows, cloud bands, and temperature clues before making any claim.
phaseModules.teacherModel: A strong forecast starts with observations, then uses patterns to make a cautious prediction.
phaseModules.visualSupport: A map-style weather visual with pressure zones, wind arrows, clouds, and temperature bands.
phaseModules.successCheck: The learner can point to two data clues in the map.

phaseModules.title: Break a forecast into parts
phaseModules.studentAction: Sort the work into observation, pattern, claim, confidence, and missing data.
phaseModules.teacherModel: Observation is what the data shows. Prediction is what may happen next. Confidence depends on how much useful evidence you have.
phaseModules.successCheck: The learner can explain why one symbol alone is weak evidence.

phaseModules.title: Build a two-evidence forecast
phaseModules.studentAction: Use the interactive check and write a first forecast sentence with because plus two data points.
phaseModules.teacherModel: Match symbols on a weather map to observations.
phaseModules.successCheck: The learner attempts the widget and writes a first evidence sentence.

phaseModules.title: Defend the forecast
phaseModules.studentAction: Write the claim, evidence, and the exact part that still feels uncertain.
phaseModules.teacherModel: Good scientists name uncertainty so they can test and revise the rule later.
phaseModules.successCheck: The learner can explain what evidence supports the claim and what data is missing.

phaseModules.title: Complete the mission checkpoint
phaseModules.studentAction: Answer the weather evidence questions without final-answer help.
phaseModules.successCheck: The learner answers the checkpoint and reviews the reasoning notes.

phaseModules.title: Save it to Memory Vault
phaseModules.studentAction: Return later to recall what pressure and wind clues can show.
phaseModules.successCheck: Delayed recall is scheduled before durable mastery is claimed.

phaseModules.title: Forecast a new place
phaseModules.studentAction: Use a new weather table or family weather board to make, test, and revise a forecast rule.
phaseModules.successCheck: The learner applies evidence reasoning to a changed map, city, or week.

phaseModules.title: Choose the next instructional move
phaseModules.studentAction: If the evidence sentence is weak, switch to one-variable reteach; if it is strong, move to a new forecast challenge.
phaseModules.successCheck: The next action is based on the evidence, not just the score.

proofTasks.prompt: Name two types of weather data that can support a short-term forecast.
Explain why one weather symbol is weaker than two connected data points.
Write a forecast claim with two evidence points and a confidence rating.
After a delay, recall how pressure or wind evidence can affect a forecast.
Use a different weather map or one-week family weather board to revise a forecast rule.

feedbackRules.result: The forecast claim uses too little or weak evidence.
feedbackRules.hint: Point to two data clues before writing the word because.
feedbackRules.action: Return to the map and label observation, pattern, and claim.

feedbackRules.result: The learner is mixing up pressure, wind, temperature, or humidity.
feedbackRules.hint: Use one variable at a time and say what it can help predict.
feedbackRules.action: Run the one-variable reteach path before combining data.

feedbackRules.result: The learner sounds too certain when evidence is incomplete.
feedbackRules.hint: Name what data is missing and lower the confidence rating.
feedbackRules.action: Revise the forecast with a confidence sentence.

reteachPaths.trigger: The learner cannot connect a data clue to a forecast claim.
reteachPaths.action: Use one variable at a time: pressure first, then wind, then temperature.

reteachPaths.trigger: The learner gives a prediction without because plus evidence.
reteachPaths.action: Use the sentence frame: I predict ___ because the map shows ___ and ___.

prerequisiteRepairPaths.trigger: The learner cannot read the map or table symbols.
prerequisiteRepairPaths.action: Repair map-symbol reading before asking for a full forecast.

challengePaths.trigger: The learner can defend a current-context forecast independently.
challengePaths.action: Give a new city or one-week family weather board and require a revised forecast rule.

transferTask.title: Family weather board
transferTask.prompt: Submit a one-week weather board with predictions, actuals, and one improved forecast rule.
transferTask.individualAccountability: Each learner submits one revised forecast rule and explains what changed.

parentTeacherNotes: This native V3 exemplar should be used to test the Bridge Academy class-session model, group evidence roles, delayed recall, and transfer before scaling Grade 6 content.
accessibilityNotes: Provide alt text for map visuals and do not rely on color alone for pressure or wind symbols.
Offer sentence frames for claim-evidence-reasoning responses.
Allow oral explanation or diagram annotation when writing is not the target skill.
safetyNotes: Do not represent forecasts as guaranteed weather or emergency guidance.
